nh_the_chasm.blurb: A small cluster of big boulders tucked into the Swamp Boulders section of Pawtuckaway State Park. Four neighbouring blocks that read as one giant stone split apart, with a narrow corridor running through the middle that gives access to most lines. Bouldering only, around twenty problems from V2 up to a single V10, bunching near V4 with a solid handful of harder lines between V6 and V8. It feels more secluded than the park's busier boulder fields, and finding it means following faint climber trails and a streambed rather than a signed path, so it suits a day of exploring more than a quick lap.

_expect.name: The Beast Alcove and Refuse Area

nh_beast_alcove_and_refuse_area_the.blurb: A crack-and-corner section of Cathedral Ledge above North Conway, set on a ledge above a slab and reached by scrambling up a step from the base trail. Mostly traditional lines, with a couple of bolted routes and one aid line, spanning an easy 5.5 up to the low 5.12s and weighted toward 5.10 and 5.11. The recessed alcove gives it a distinct feel, and the start of the main alcove line tends to stay dry when it rains. Expect fewer parties here than on the nearby slabs, and a granite cliff that is best in fall; spring seepage is common.

nh_lower_left_wall_ventilator_slabs.blurb: The left-hand base of Cathedral Ledge in North Conway, best known for slab climbing that rewards precise footwork over pulling hard. About twenty routes, nearly all traditional with a lone bolted line and one aid route, running from a friendly 5.7 up through the 5.10s and 5.11s to a single 5.12. Some of the thinner faces carry little protection and feel serious, while a few easier lines make good starters; the popular ones get busy on weekends. The ledge itself gets afternoon shade in summer, and fall is the favoured season.

nj_witherspoon_woods_boulders.blurb: A low-key bouldering spot in the woods beside Princeton, in central New Jersey. Roughly two dozen problems on scattered boulders and talus, so it rewards a bit of imagination and wandering rather than offering a polished circuit. Difficulty runs from V0 to V9, but most of the lines are in the V0 to V3 range, which makes it friendly for beginners and for warming up, with only a few problems at V4 and above. Quiet and unassuming, it sits in forest at modest elevation, and summers can be humid and buggy.

nj_devil_s_half_acre.blurb: The best-known boulder field in Sourland Mountain Preserve in Somerset County, New Jersey. Very large boulders are strewn through open woods on the mountainside, and a hiking trail winds right over and around them. About twenty problems, entirely bouldering, from V0 to V5: a broad middle of V1 to V3 with a few harder moves at V4 and V5, so it works for mixed groups. The setting is wooded and rugged, with big blocks and the odd tree growing from a split. Spring brings wildflowers along the walk in.

nm_area_37.blurb: A small sport crag in the Jemez Mountains of northern New Mexico, around 8,600 feet and roughly a mile east of Las Conchas. Nearly thirty routes on rhyolite, all sport except for one crack line, with grades from 5.7 to 5.12 and the bulk of the climbing in the 5.10 to 5.12 range. A handful of easier routes round it out. The wall sits partly hidden among trees, and the walk from the road is so short that it fits a quick session or a stop alongside other Jemez crags.
